summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. The United Kingdom reserves defence and external affairs, while local ordinance governs the constitutional, criminal and family law that a visitor would deal with on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex faces no criminalisation exposure under local law.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 made same-sex marriage legal on 14 May 2015 and defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. That definition is the only express reference to gender identity in the territory's legislation recorded in these sources. The ordinance was approved unanimously by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside the Pitcairn Islands, so a partnership or marriage entered abroad is recorded as recognised locally.

No incident of violence targeting a trans person is documented for the Pitcairn Islands in these sources, and no dated case of any kind appears in the record.
tangentialFactors:
The territory has roughly 50 residents, and none of them is known to be in a same-sex relationship. In a community of that size, a visitor's presence and presentation are visible to the whole population, and the sources offer no account of how gender-nonconforming visitors are received socially.

The territory's discrimination guarantee and its marriage law are the two instruments that carry weight for a trans visitor, and they differ in scope: the constitution covers sexual orientation only, while the 2015 marriage definition expressly covers gender identity. A trans visitor therefore has a stronger textual position on relationship recognition than on discrimination.

The sources rank no jurisdictions and provide no comparative or per-capita figures for the Pitcairn Islands, so no comparison of risk levels between territories can be drawn from this record.
localsOnly:
Adoption has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

The anti-discrimination guarantee in the Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 operates for residents as a constitutional protection on sexual-orientation grounds; it does not create an offence and does not name gender identity.

Residents may register a civil partnership performed outside the Pitcairn Islands under the Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015.

None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship, so no local pattern of partnered same-sex residents is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether a procedure exists in the Pitcairn Islands for changing a registered gender marker is unresolved: the sources describe no such process, its requirements or its availability to residents and visitors, and its absence cannot be confirmed from this record.

No source in this inventory addresses airport or port screening, document markers, gender-affirming healthcare access, or access to gendered facilities in the Pitcairn Islands. Nothing is documented either way on these points.

No trans-specific violence figure, survey of trans residents or dated incident is available for the Pitcairn Islands, so no prevalence statement about present conditions can be made from this record. The absence of documented cases is not evidence of their absence in practice.

Military service is a United Kingdom responsibility and is carried at the parent level rather than in this territory record.
